What's your origin story? What got you into cycling, where'd you start and where are you now? Tell your story!

I bought a junky single-speed to ride in DC when I first started working there. Before too long I found myself going for rides at lunch just to see the sights, then I wanted to go farther in that hour. I bought a decent single to ride, and have upgraded it over several years. Now I go out on some trails on the weekends, put in as many miles during the week as possible, and thoroughly enjoy riding.

I started 2 years ago as a bike commuter on an old mountain bike I had to save money (sold my car). 16 mile round trip, clocked over 2500 miles in the first year alone, lost 30 pounds (5'6" 160 -> 130), learned to service and care for my own bikes, started getting active in the bike communities and civil community to push bike/ped transit.

Now I'm an avid commuter and help others in my company and in the community go on their first ride in my free time. I'd like to go on some multi-day bikecamping for the first time this fall but gotta get around to planning that out!
Sounds similar to be, was really surprised how easy it is to get fit by just bike committing.

Got into BMX riding (freestyle) around 13 years old, definitely my favorite type of riding and still ride BMX a lot .. started working in a bike shop when I was about 23 and got the MTB bug, started riding trail and DH, got into road riding around the same time, but I only ride for recreation and commuting, could never be bothered with the stress of competing. I love bike riding in all it's forms and nothing beats the feeling of just being on a bike. Many injuries over the years but you gotta take the good with the bad. Knocking on 30's door and still get all giddy when I get a new bike. It never ends. I ♥ bikes.

I just wish my non cyclist friends could be a little more mature about me wearing lycra, and stop telling me what I could have bought with the money spent on my bike collection :D

started when I was 6 or 7. I learned how to ride it alone. I then moved to a big city when I was 9, and I rapidly grew too big for that bike. it's only 15 years later that I found a bike good enough for what I thought I wanted (meanwhile, I was using inline skates). I bought a 3-speed internal hub bike last year, belt drive. rode it for a few months, then I got bored. I changed it to a fixed gear just last week, and I'm very happy with the transformation! it's a different experience, and I'm always looking for reasons to ride now.
How in earth did you learn to ride a bike yourself???
at that age it's easy, and painful. all I remember is being alone in an open space with my bike, falling often, and even hitting a parked police car...

I moved house and was close enough to work to feel embarrassed about driving but started really early in the morning so didn't want to walk and have to get up even earlier so got a second hand bike. By the time I moved again I upgraded to a road bike and this year joined the local club and have been riding more than ever.

It's a great feeling to think about how much progress I've made with fitness and ability in a relatively short time.

Went backpacking and saw some people mountain biking. It looked like fun, so I decided to buy a cheap mountain bike. I wouldn't say I was hooked right away, but I liked it enough to keep doing it until I got good enough to where it started getting fun.

I took up road biking when I moved to Chicago and had nowhere to mountain bike. I picked up an old schwinn collegiate and got to really enjoy heading out from my house instead of driving to a trail.

I lived on my BMX when I was a kid (Late 80's Early 90's) we would cruise around the Neighbourhood. Ride to each others houses or the local shops. We all wanted to be BMX bandits.

Progress to Riding to School or just using a bike as transport in you early to Late teens, and it just klind of kept going from there. I've always had a bike, and always ridden at least once or twice a month, out of neccesity, or for fun. Started lookign for a way to get fit and the bike was the obvious option.

I started to bicycle commute in 2012 after being inspired by a couple of colleagues at work. We are lucky enough to have a locker room with showers in our building, so commuting even during a rainy day or winter is no problem when you have dry clothes and a hot shower waiting for you.

After about two weeks I retired by good ol' 15 year old sitting-in-the-garage mountain bike and purchased a hybrid Trek 7.3 FX. After 6 months on that, I purchased a Merida Cyclo Cross 4-MD instead, because I wanted disc brakes and road bike gears and handlebars while commuting. I still use this after three years.

Two years ago I also got a hold of an old Miyata 710 which I brought back into shape, and this is now my "sunday cabriolet" bicycle. I'm only using it when the weather is nice, to/from work and on weekend rides.

The part I like best is that I feel really refreshed at work after a ride in the morning. Also I save a fair amount money since the toll passes and city parking are expensive. Buses are expensive in my area as well. Honestly, I can afford both the car and bus options (I take the bus sometimes), but I like riding the bike. Keeps me healthy.

This is what my commute often feels like

Late to the party, but I just discovered this sub.

My mom married a guy who did BMX (like, national competition level) when I was 9. I hadn't yet learned to ride a bike. That changed quickly. So from 9 to around 14 I was riding mountain bikes, getting better at small jumps and things like that, just having fun. At 14, I got a job as a bike builder at the local bike shop. I saved up a bit and bought my first road bike (Giant OCR1) and absolutely fell in love. I rode road all through high school and at the start of college, before life happened and my beloved OCR was sold.

Fast forward 8 years to about six weeks ago, I went on a bike ride on a friend's bike and remembered how much I loved riding. Two weeks later I bought a Trek FX 7.3, and while I'm still getting used to not having drop bars, and the lack of long bike paths here, I'm loving it all over again. I'm planning to be on the FX through the winter, and then upgrade to a dedicated road bike next spring.

I only got into cycling 7 or 8 months ago. I saw someone who was really lean, saw he was big into cycling, and decided to give it a try to see if I could get similar results. Turns out that I really enjoy it. It's now one of the biggest parts of my life. And it's also helped me get nice and lean, but at this point I consider that a bonus.

I've yet to buy a "real" bike. I started off with a cheap walmart mountain bike on which I swapped the tires out for thinner road tires. From that I moved on to a cheap walmart road bike with drop bars and stem mounted shifters. Both bikes are way heavier than they should be and have had serious issues once I started putting serious mileage on them, and that's of course because they're made from cheap crap. But I still managed to get a lot out of them so far.

I now do around 100 miles a week, give or take. I've also learned a lot about how to do my own maintenance, but I still often rely on my LBS for advice. They seem happy to give me information as long as I'm buying my parts and tools from them. It's still the busy season, so they're backed up anyway. During fall and winter they'd probably be less likely to be so helpful with repair advice, because from what I gather, it gets very slow and they'd probably prefer the extra money they'd get from the labor cost.

Eventually I'll buy a real bike. Most likely a touring bike with some nice fenders, drop bars, proper shifters, and a compact crank. I haven't decided yet whether it'll have skinny tires or wide ones. I love the cushy soft floaty feel of nice wide tires, but I also love the relative ease of peddling thinner tires. Meanwhile I'm doing great with my heavy ass road bike, having replaced basically the entire drive train and the tires. It may be heavy but it rides good and I can still regularly beat guys in lycra up a hill climb (they still manage to kick my ass on the descents despite being on lighter bikes, and this I think is because they're more aerodynamic and have thinner tires), so I'm not terribly concerned about the extra weight. I love a good hill climb. I'm terrible at sprinting, though. I also see no reason to switch to clipless pedals instead of the regular flat pegs. People say they're more efficient, but the guys at gcn found no evidence for that when they compared the two. Besides, I think I prefer to be able to wear normal shoes, especially if I am out shopping.
